Isaiah.author: Isaiah son of Amoz is the named prophet; many scholars debate how the book reached its final form and whether later sections involve additional prophetic voices or disciples.
Isaiah.audience: Judah and Jerusalem across periods of Assyrian threat, judgment, exile-related hope, and anticipated restoration.
Isaiah.purpose: To confront Judah's sin, announce judgment, reveal God's holiness and sovereignty, and proclaim future restoration and hope.
Isaiah.theme: The Holy One of Israel judges sin yet promises salvation, restoration, and a future righteous ruler and servant.
Isaiah.summary: Isaiah moves between severe warnings and sweeping hope. It confronts idolatry and injustice, promises a coming king and servant, and looks toward renewed creation and restored Zion.

movements.title: Judgment, Isaiah's Call, and the Assyrian Crisis
movements.description: Isaiah indicts Judah's sin, encounters God's holiness in his call vision, and ministers during Judah's conflict with Assyria.

movements.title: Comfort and Return
movements.description: The book announces comfort, God's incomparable rule, and hope for return from exile.

movements.title: Servant, Restoration, and New Creation
movements.description: Servant songs, salvation promises, and visions of renewed Zion and creation dominate the closing sections.

keyFigures.name: Isaiah
keyFigures.description: The prophet son of Amoz, who sees the LORD enthroned and ministers in Jerusalem for decades.

keyFigures.name: Uzziah
keyFigures.description: King of Judah in the year of whose death Isaiah receives his call vision.

keyFigures.name: Ahaz
keyFigures.description: King of Judah who refuses to trust God during the Syro-Ephraimite crisis and is given the Immanuel sign.

keyFigures.name: Hezekiah
keyFigures.description: King of Judah who seeks the LORD when Assyria besieges Jerusalem.

keyFigures.name: Sennacherib
keyFigures.description: King of Assyria whose army threatens Jerusalem and is struck down.

keyFigures.name: Cyrus
keyFigures.description: The Persian king named as the LORD's anointed instrument to free the exiles.

keyFigures.name: The Servant of the LORD
keyFigures.description: The figure of the Servant Songs who brings justice and suffers for others; the New Testament identifies him with Jesus.

Jeremiah.author: Jeremiah son of Hilkiah, with assistance from the scribe Baruch in preserving and transmitting his messages.
Jeremiah.audience: Judah and Jerusalem in the final decades before and during Babylonian conquest.
Jeremiah.purpose: To warn Judah of coming judgment for covenant rebellion, call for repentance, and promise eventual restoration and a new covenant.
Jeremiah.theme: Persistent rebellion brings judgment, yet God promises restoration and a new covenant written on the heart.
Jeremiah.summary: Jeremiah spends decades warning Judah that Babylonian conquest is coming. He suffers rejection, witnesses Jerusalem's fall, and still proclaims hope for restoration and a new covenant.

movements.title: Jeremiah's Call and Warnings
movements.description: Jeremiah is appointed as a prophet and repeatedly warns Judah to turn from idolatry and injustice.

movements.title: Conflict and Persecution
movements.description: Jeremiah faces priests, prophets, kings, imprisonment, and public hostility over his message.

movements.title: Fall of Jerusalem and New Covenant Hope
movements.description: Jeremiah announces restoration and a new covenant, Jerusalem falls to Babylon, and the book closes with oracles against the nations and an account of the city's fall.

keyFigures.name: Jeremiah
keyFigures.description: The 'weeping prophet,' called as a youth to warn Judah of coming judgment.

keyFigures.name: Baruch
keyFigures.description: Jeremiah's scribe and companion, who records and reads his messages.

keyFigures.name: Josiah
keyFigures.description: The reforming king during whose reign Jeremiah's ministry begins.

keyFigures.name: Jehoiakim
keyFigures.description: King of Judah who burns Jeremiah's scroll in defiance.

keyFigures.name: Zedekiah
keyFigures.description: Judah's last king, who consults Jeremiah secretly but refuses to obey.

keyFigures.name: Hananiah
keyFigures.description: A false prophet who contradicts Jeremiah and dies within the year as Jeremiah foretold.

keyFigures.name: Ebed-melech
keyFigures.description: A Cushite official who rescues Jeremiah from a muddy cistern.

keyFigures.name: Gedaliah
keyFigures.description: Governor appointed by Babylon after Jerusalem's fall, who is assassinated.

keyFigures.name: Nebuchadnezzar
keyFigures.description: King of Babylon, whom Jeremiah calls God's servant in bringing judgment on Judah.

Lamentations.author: Anonymous; traditionally associated with Jeremiah, though the book itself does not name him.
Lamentations.audience: The devastated community of Judah after Jerusalem's fall.
Lamentations.purpose: To give poetic voice to grief over Jerusalem's destruction while preserving confession, prayer, and hope in God's mercy.
Lamentations.theme: Faith can lament honestly in catastrophe while still appealing to God's compassion and faithfulness.
Lamentations.summary: Lamentations is a collection of five poems grieving Jerusalem's destruction. It refuses easy answers, acknowledges sin and judgment, and still looks to God's mercies as a basis for hope.

movements.title: Jerusalem Mourned
movements.description: The city is personified as a grieving widow after destruction and exile.

movements.title: Judgment and Deep Suffering
movements.description: The poems describe siege, hunger, violence, and the experience of divine judgment.

movements.title: Hope in the Middle of Grief
movements.description: The central poem recalls God's steadfast mercy even while suffering continues.

keyFigures.name: Jeremiah (traditional author)
keyFigures.description: Long associated with the book, though the poems themselves do not name their author.

keyFigures.name: Daughter Zion
keyFigures.description: Jerusalem personified as a grieving widow who mourns her children and her ruin.

keyFigures.name: The man who has seen affliction
keyFigures.description: The individual voice of chapter 3, who moves from deep suffering to hope in God's mercies.

Ezekiel.author: Ezekiel, a priest and prophet among the exiles in Babylon.
Ezekiel.audience: Judean exiles in Babylon before and after Jerusalem's destruction.
Ezekiel.purpose: To explain judgment on Jerusalem, defend God's justice, call for repentance, and proclaim future restoration and renewed divine presence.
Ezekiel.theme: God's glory is not confined to Jerusalem; He judges rebellion, gives new life, and promises restored presence among His people.
Ezekiel.summary: Ezekiel receives dramatic visions and symbolic acts announcing Jerusalem's fall. After the city is destroyed, his message turns strongly toward restoration, new hearts, revived people, and a renewed temple vision.

movements.title: Vision and Call
movements.description: Ezekiel sees God's mobile throne and is commissioned as a watchman to the exiles.

movements.title: Jerusalem's Judgment
movements.description: Symbolic actions and visions announce the city's corruption and coming destruction.

movements.title: Restoration Visions
movements.description: The valley of dry bones, reunited people, and temple vision depict future renewal and God's returning presence.

keyFigures.name: Ezekiel
keyFigures.description: A priest exiled to Babylon, called as a prophet and watchman through dramatic visions.

keyFigures.name: Jehoiachin
keyFigures.description: The exiled king of Judah, from whose deportation Ezekiel dates his prophecies.

keyFigures.name: The elders of Israel
keyFigures.description: Exiled leaders who come to Ezekiel for counsel and are confronted about their idolatry.

keyFigures.name: Ezekiel's wife
keyFigures.description: Her sudden death becomes a sign of the coming loss of the temple.

keyFigures.name: The shepherd prince
keyFigures.description: A future ruler from David's line whom God promises to set over His restored people.

keyFigures.name: Gog of Magog
keyFigures.description: A symbolic enemy leader whose final assault against God's people is defeated.

Daniel.author: The book centers on Daniel, a Judean exile; Jewish and Christian traditions differ with some modern scholars over the date and composition of the final book.
Daniel.audience: Jews living under foreign empires and facing pressure to compromise.
Daniel.purpose: To encourage faithful endurance by showing God's sovereignty over kings, empires, persecution, and history.
Daniel.theme: God rules over human empires and will ultimately establish His kingdom, so His people can remain faithful under pressure.
Daniel.summary: Daniel combines court stories of faithful Jews in exile with symbolic visions about kingdoms, persecution, judgment, and God's final rule.

movements.title: Faithfulness in Babylon
movements.description: Daniel and his friends resist assimilation pressures while serving in foreign courts.

movements.title: Fiery Furnace and Lions' Den
movements.description: Daniel's friends and Daniel himself face death for refusing to compromise worship and prayer.

movements.title: Apocalyptic Visions
movements.description: Daniel sees symbolic visions of beasts, kingdoms, heavenly judgment, and future deliverance.

keyFigures.name: Daniel
keyFigures.description: A Judean exile, renamed Belteshazzar, who stays faithful in the Babylonian and Persian courts and receives visions.

keyFigures.name: Shadrach, Meshach, and Abednego
keyFigures.description: Daniel's companions (Hananiah, Mishael, and Azariah), who refuse to worship the king's image and are delivered from the furnace.

keyFigures.name: Nebuchadnezzar
keyFigures.description: King of Babylon, humbled by God until he acknowledges the Most High.

keyFigures.name: Belshazzar
keyFigures.description: Babylonian ruler who sees the writing on the wall the night his kingdom falls.

keyFigures.name: Darius the Mede
keyFigures.description: The ruler under whom Daniel is thrown into the lions' den.

keyFigures.name: Gabriel and Michael
keyFigures.description: Angels who appear in the visions: Gabriel interprets them, and Michael is described as a prince who protects Daniel's people.

keyFigures.name: One like a son of man
keyFigures.description: A heavenly figure who receives everlasting dominion from the Ancient of Days; Jesus applies this title to Himself.
